title: Online Tutoring
subtitle: Turn what you know into a clear learning result, not a 60-minute screen share with excellent intentions

blocks.text: Knowing algebra and teaching algebra are cousins, not twins. One solves for x; the other calmly explains why x keeps leaving the house without telling anyone.

Online tutoring is a service business built around one kind of learner, one subject and a result you can see. A strong tutor does not promise grades. They find the starting point, teach one skill, check that it stuck and share progress. When working with children, a tutor also needs a parent’s consent, safe messaging rules and technology that protects privacy.
A narrow offer is easier to sell and deliver: for example, Grade 9 Ontario math problem solving, or CELPIP speaking feedback. Not “all subjects, all ages, all planets.”

items.title: “A tutor must know every answer immediately.”
items.text: A good tutor can pause, check and show how to find an answer. Confidently inventing a formula is performance art, not teaching.

blocks.text: Canada: Starting a business
A focused tutoring offer is easier to sell, easier to teach and easier to charge fairly for.
blocks.detail: Picking one learner, one subject and one result to show turns what you know into steady paid sessions.
blocks.extra: Section 02 shows how to sell progress people can see.

sections.title: Sell Progress That Can Be Observed

blocks.text: A tutoring offer becomes sellable the moment progress can be shown, not just felt.

items.title: LEARNER
items.text: Choose an age group, curriculum, exam, language level or work skill you can teach accurately.

items.title: STARTING POINT
items.text: Use a short skills check, some sample work and a conversation. Do not turn the first meeting into an ambush exam with dramatic music.

items.title: RESULT
items.text: Describe what the learner should be able to do: solve one type of problem, organize an essay, explain an idea or raise a practice score.

items.title: PROOF
items.text: Compare attempts, common mistakes, finished practice and how the learner explains things. Grades matter, but more than tutoring affects them.

blocks.text: A useful 60-minute session can follow five steps: check in, recall what was learned last time, show one skill, practise it with feedback and set a small next step.
For children, keep consent, scheduling and payment with a parent or guardian. Agree on recording, messaging, missed sessions and who gets progress updates.

items.title: “More worksheets automatically create more learning.”
items.text: Practice helps when it targets the learner’s real mistake and comes with feedback. A 42-page packet can also become an effective coaster.

blocks.text: OPC: Privacy and educational technology

sections.title: Build the Business Around the Lesson

blocks.text: Price the whole service: planning, teaching, feedback, platform fees, payment fees, materials, bookkeeping, cancellations and messages.

items.title: Terms in writing
items.text: Your rate, packages, payment timing, and rules for cancelling and rescheduling, sent before the first paid session.

items.title: Materials you are allowed to use
items.text: Use your own worksheets, free licensed resources or the student’s own textbook. Copying and selling a publisher’s pages breaks copyright.

items.title: Marketing messages with consent
items.text: Canada’s Anti-Spam Legislation (CASL) means you need permission before you send promotional emails or texts, plus a clear way to unsubscribe.

items.title: Records
items.text: Keep a log of sessions, invoices and payments. It supports your taxes and settles any billing questions.

blocks.text: Tutoring that follows a provincial curriculum, or that supports some credit courses or prerequisites, may be exempt from GST/HST. Other teaching may be taxable. The word “tutor” does not decide the answer.
The $30,000 small supplier limit counts taxable sales, not exempt tutoring income. Find out which kind of service you sell before you use that limit.
Tax basics for your first year

items.title: REPORT IT
items.text: Business income goes on Form T2125 with your personal tax return, whether clients pay by cash, cheque or e-transfer.

items.title: PAY BOTH HALVES OF CPP
items.text: Self-employed people pay the worker and employer shares of CPP, 11.9% of net business income above the basic amount, on Schedule 8 of the return.

items.title: SET MONEY ASIDE
items.text: Nobody takes tax off your pay. Move a share of every payment into a separate account. If you owe more than $3,000 ($1,800 in Quebec) this year and in either of the last two years, the CRA will ask for quarterly instalments.

items.title: KEEP RECORDS SIX YEARS
items.text: Keep invoices, receipts, mileage and bank records for six years from the end of the tax year they belong to.

items.title: “All tutoring is automatically GST/HST-exempt.”
items.text: The exemption depends on what you teach and how it links to a provincial curriculum, a credit course or a qualifying prerequisite. Check the actual service.

blocks.text: Key takeaway: a tutoring business earns trust by narrowing the offer, checking before teaching, measuring one clear result, protecting young learners and working with written rules for pricing, privacy, copyright and cancellations.

sections.title: Eli Teaches Less and Learns More

blocks.text: Meet Eli
paragraphs: Eli Tremblay starts tutoring high school math online from Moncton. His goal is ten paying students by September. His first ad offers calculus, chemistry, essay writing and “general academic confidence.” It sounds impressive, and slightly like four businesses sharing one trench coat.
His first student is Sophie, in Grade 9. Eli prepares a full hour of advanced equations to show what he can do.
Ten minutes in, he notices something. Sophie understands the ideas, but she keeps dropping minus signs when she moves terms across the equals sign. That one habit is costing her most of her marks.
Eli has a choice. Stick to his impressive plan, or throw it out and work on the minus signs. He decides to throw it out. He gives her three short problems and asks her to explain each step out loud.
Together they build a one-page sign check she can use on every test. Eli sends her mother a short note: the skill they worked on, what he saw and what comes next.
The twist comes two weeks later. Sophie’s mother tells three other parents about the sign check. They all have Grade 9 or 10 kids, and none of them need chemistry.
Eli rewrites his ad around Grade 9 and 10 math problem solving. By September he has eleven students. His slogan is not literally “fewer subjects, fewer trench coats,” but the idea holds up.

blocks.text: The first session should give a small win and a clear next step. A learner who understands the plan is more likely to practise between sessions.
What resolved the conflict?
A narrower offer found the real mistake, instead of piling more content on top of it.
Eli filled his schedule by fixing one small mistake well instead of teaching everything at once.
blocks.detail: Teaching one clear skill, and showing parents the proof, can grow your own tutoring business the same way.
blocks.extra: The quick check in Section 05 tests whether you can spot the next move.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Why is a narrow tutoring offer easier to run?
items.detail: It is easier to sell and to teach, because you can support one age group, curriculum, exam or skill well instead of promising every subject to everyone.

items.title: What should happen before you choose the lesson?
items.detail: A short skills check, some sample work and a conversation to find the starting point.

items.title: Why should you never promise grades?
items.detail: Grades show progress, but more than tutoring affects them. Describe a skill the learner will be able to show instead.

items.title: What privacy rules matter when tutoring a child?
items.detail: A parent’s consent, with scheduling and payment kept with an adult, plus agreed rules on recording, messaging and progress updates.

items.title: Why must you check GST/HST instead of assuming?
items.detail: The exemption depends on what you teach and how it links to a provincial curriculum, credit course or qualifying prerequisite, not on the word “tutor.”

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): First Student Learning Plan

blocks.text: Describe learners in general terms. Do not write a child’s full name, school login, birth date, private test results or meeting passwords here.

Keep progress notes short: the skill you worked on, what you saw, the feedback you gave and the next step. Test your offer: can you explain the learner, problem, result, session format and price in two sentences?

items.title: Diagnostic
items.text: A short check to find where a learner is starting.

items.title: Learning outcome
items.text: A specific skill the learner should be able to show.

items.title: Session arc
items.text: A repeatable set of steps for each lesson.

items.title: Retrieval practice
items.text: Recalling what you learned before looking at the answer.

items.title: Progress note
items.text: A short record of what you saw, the feedback and the next step.

items.title: Exempt supply
items.text: A service you generally do not charge GST/HST on.

items.title: CASL
items.text: Canada’s Anti-Spam Legislation, the rules for commercial emails and texts.

quiz.question: True or False: “A tutor must know every answer immediately.”

questions: Who is your learner, what subject and level, and what is one result they will be able to show?
How will you find their starting point in the first session?
What will you charge, and what are your cancellation and rescheduling rules?
How will you share progress, and with whom? For a child, name the parent or guardian contact.
Is your tutoring likely exempt from GST/HST, or taxable? (Exempt / Taxable / Not sure yet)
Where will you find your first three students?
samples: Grade 9 and 10 students in Ontario math. Solve multi-step equations without sign errors.
Three short problems and a chat about what feels hard.
$45 an hour, or five sessions for $200. 24 hours’ notice to cancel.
A short email to the parent after every session.
Not sure yet. I will check whether it follows the provincial curriculum.
A school parent group, a community centre board and two friends with teens.
